question.leadin: In 1962, this man was imprisoned for life at Robben Island.
question.text: Name this civil rights leader who became the first black president of South Africa.
question.clue: This man evaded capture by police by pretending to be a cook and gardener on Liliesleaf Farm, which later led to his imprisonment with 19 others in what became known as the Rivonia Trial.

swap.text: The Jameson Raid was an attempt to take over this largest city in South Africa.
swap.clue: Mandela posed as a farm worker at Liliesleaf Farm, located in this city, which was eventually raided leading to his capture and trial. The Soweto uprising occurred in this city, the largest in its country, after the introduction of Afrikaans.

question.text: In this nation that is plagued by hyperinflation, Morgan Tsvangirai and Robert Mugabe reached a power sharing deal in 2008 after allegations of election fraud.
question.clue: This country's first president was Canaan Banana, who was arrested in 1997 on charges of sodomy.

swap.text: Gaddafi led this North African country, which disputed the Aouzou Strip with its southern neighbor, Chad. The U.S. embassy in this country's city of Benghazi was attacked in 2012.
swap.clue: This country was formerly called an Arab Jamahiriya and had an all-green flag.

question.text: This member of the Kapenguria Six was the first president of an independent Kenya. This man, whose last name can be translated as "the light of Kenya," was succeeded by Daniel arap Moi.
question.clue: He banned the opposition KPU party following 1969 elections, after which Oginga Odinga became his Vice President.

swap.text: South Africa objected to the UN Trust Territory status of this modern country, then known as South-West Africa. It gained independence from South Africa in 1990, after a twenty-year guerilla war.
swap.answerHtml: Republic of Namibia [or Republiek van Namibië; or Republik Namibia]
swap.clue: This country was ceded Walvis Bay in 1994, and fought a brief secession movement in the Caprivi Strip.

question.leadin: Patrice Lumumba, the first elected Prime Minister of this country, was soon deposed and assassinated, making the CIA real glad.
question.text: Name this large country which was renamed Zaire during the 32-year reign of the Africanizing dictator Mobutu Sese Seko.
question.answerHtml: Democratic Republic of the Congo [or DRC; or DR-Congo; or Congo-Kinshasa; prompt on "Congo"; do NOT accept or prompt on "Republic of the Congo"]
question.clue: Moise Tshombe led the secessionist Katanga province.

swap.text: A president of this country, Abdirashid Shermarke, was assassinated by a bodyguard, leading to the takeover of Siad Barre, who led this country's invasion of nearby Ethiopia in the Ogaden War.
swap.answerHtml: Somalia [or Federal Republic of Somalia; or Jamhuuriyadda Federaalka Soomaaliya]
swap.clue: After the dictator Siad Barre was ousted from power in this nation, warlords began to take control of autonomous regions such as Puntland.

question.leadin: The Underground Railroad wasn't a disaster, but answer these questions about incidents what were.
question.text: In this African country, 192 people were killed and at least 160 more injured in a June 2002 accident at Moamba.
question.clue: A right-wing organization opposing the socialist government of this country drew support from such cities as the Beira port in Sofala province, was formed by Andre Matsangaissa, and laid down its arms in the 1990s following the Rome Accords.

swap.leadin: A one-time kabaka or king of this modern-day nation was called "King Freddie" by British newspapers and was exiled for two years until he returned as a constitutional monarch.
swap.text: Identify this country where Mutesa II held power after it gained independence. This country underwent a "Move to the Left" under Milton Obote.
swap.clue: A 2012 documentary was released by Invisible Children to combat this country's Lord's Resistance Army, led by Joseph Kony.

question.text: This great Zulu ruler reorganized the army and led the Mfecane, or "Crushing." He died shortly after the arrival of Europeans in southern Africa.
question.clue: His army gained ground by "scattering" rivals and incorporating them into his state.

swap.leadin: This kingdom collapsed after a defeat by the French at the Battle of Poguessa.
swap.text: Name this African kingdom that ruled over the Fon people and was a leading supplier of slaves to European empires. It was located in present day Benin.
swap.clue: The city of Allada, the home of this empire's founder Do-Aklin, was captured by its king Adaja.

question.text: This city, whose name means "city of a thousand" is the capital of Madagascar.
question.clue: One woman who ruled from this city applied a trial by ordeal involving eating toxic tangena nuts en masse.

swap.leadin: In the early 18th century, this empire recruited scouts to clear brush, blaze false trails, and drain standing water based on medical expertise that included a precursor of germ theory.
swap.text: Name this empire whose founder Osei Tutu ("OH-say TOO-too") modernized its army with tactics he learned from the Akwamuhene ("ah-KWAH-moo-hay-nay"). Many houses had indoor plumbing in this empire's city of Kumasi.
swap.clue: This state's unifier founded his capital on the site where a Kum tree planted by the priest Okomfo Anokyo prospered; that king, who also defeated the Denkyira, was Osei Tutu.

question.text: This queen from the Zenata succeeded Kusaila as leader of the Berber resistance. Although her victory at the 698 Battle of Meskiana was absolute, whether she was pagan, Christian, or Jewish remains uncertain to this day.
question.clue: This mysterious "Queen of the Berbers" led revolts in North Africa against the Umayyads in the 7th century AD, and was given a name meaning "witch," possibly for being Jewish. According to Ibn Khaldun, she caused no end of trouble for the general Hasan ibn al-Nu'man, but was eventually killed by him.

swap.leadin: Before his death, the merchant Alhassan Dantata pointed to sixty pyramids made of this good.
swap.text: Name this legume that Clement Attlee unsuccessfully attempted to grow in Tanganyika after World War II.
swap.clue: Following its introduction, this crop superseded a similar plant commonly named for the Bambara people in importance in West Africa.

question.leadin: Joshua Blahyi was nicknamed "General Butt Naked" during this conflict due to his belief that wearing no clothing made his soldiers bulletproof.
question.text: Name this conflict. Amos Sawyer served as interim president during this conflict in which the INPFL faction split from its progenitor under Prince Johnson.
question.answerHtml: First Liberian Civil War [prompt on Liberian Civil War]

swap.leadin: Al-Maghili "replied" to a series of seven "questions" posed by this ruler about the intersection of Islam and the state.
swap.text: Name this ruler who founded a namesake West African dynasty after usurping the son of Sonni 'Ali in 1493.
swap.answerHtml: Askia Muḥammad [or Askia Muhammad I; or Muḥammad ibn Abī Bakr Ture; prompt on Muḥammad; prompt on Askia dynasty]
swap.clue: This ruler stood firm against the pagan practices of his subjects and was declared the Caliph of the Western Sudan after taking a notable pilgrimage to Mecca in 1496.

question.text: This successor dynasty to the Axumite Kingdom was once ruled by a figure whose name means "The BEES Recognize His Sovereignty", Gebrel Masquel Lalibela. It was supplanted by the Solomonic dynasty.
question.clue: Its last ruler, "Za-Ilmaknun," has a name translating as "The Unknown," perhaps reflecting a damnatio memoriae by a successor dynasty founded by Yekuno Amlak.

swap.leadin: This dynasty ended when the Merenids captured Marrakech.
swap.text: Name this North African Islamic dynasty whose caliph Abu Yaqub Yusuf captured Seville in 1172. They were driven back to Africa after losing the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa.
swap.clue: This dynasty's distinctive combination of Zahiri jurisprudence and Ashʿari theology was formalized under its first politically established leader, ʿAbd al-Muʾmin.
